pages.name: Ride along line 1
pages.text: The point can only ride along line 1, so its y is always `2x + 1`. Swap that in for y in `x + y = 7` and you get `x + (2x + 1) = 7`, drawn as two bars. They match only where the point meets line 2, at the crossing (2, 5).

pages.name: Swap it in
pages.task: Line 1 is `y = x + 3` and line 2 is `2x + y = 12`. Which equation do you get by swapping line 1 into line 2?
pages.why: Line 1 says y is `x + 3`, so `x + 3` goes in place of y, inside a bracket, giving `2x + (x + 3) = 12`. Now only x is left to find.

pages.name: Your turn
pages.why: Swapping in gives `2x + (x + 3) = 12`, so `3x + 3 = 12`, `3x = 9` and x = 3. Then `y = 3 + 3 = 6`. It checks in both, as `3 + 3 = 6` and `2 × 3 + 6 = 12`.

pages.alt: A squared grid, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 14. Line 1, solid: y = x + 3. Line 2, dashed: 2x + y = 12. The point rides along line 1, at (3, 6). A ring marks where the lines cross. Beside the grid, two bars from a zero mark: 2x + (x + 3) worked out at the point is 12, beside 12, so they match.

pages.name: Between the tenths
pages.text: With `x + y = 5` the crossing falls between the tenths, so a graph can only estimate it. [[Substitution]] is exact. `3x + 1 = 5` gives x = 4/3, and the point clicks onto (4/3, 11/3).

pages.why: Swapping in gives `x + 3x = 3`, so `4x = 3` and x = 3/4. Then `y = 3 × 3/4 = 9/4`. It checks in both, as `3 × 3/4 = 9/4` and `3/4 + 9/4 = 3`.

pages.name: Make y the subject
pages.text: When neither equation starts with `y =`, rearrange one first. Either would do; here, take `2x` from both sides of `2x + y = 11` to get `y = 11 − 2x`, which shows how a minus in front of a bracket works. That minus takes away all of the bracket, so both signs inside change, and x = 4 and y = 3.

pages.alt: A squared grid, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 14. Line 1, solid: y = 11 minus  2x. Line 2, dashed: 3x minus  y = 9. The point rides along line 1, at (4, 3). A ring marks where the lines cross. Beside the grid, two bars from a zero mark: 3x minus  (11 minus  2x) worked out at the point is 9, beside 9, so they match.

pages.name: Mind the minus
pages.why: Make y the subject, `y = 7 − 2x`, and swap it in, giving `4x − (7 − 2x) = 5`. The minus changes both signs, so `4x − 7 + 2x = 5`, `6x = 12` and x = 2. Then `y = 7 − 4 = 3`, and it checks in both, as `4 + 3 = 7` and `8 − 3 = 5`.

pages.name: When the x's cancel
pages.text: Here line 2, `y − 2x = 4`, is `y = 2x + 4`, the same m as line 1, so it runs parallel. Swap in and the x's cancel, leaving `1 = 4`, false wherever the point rides: no solution, which textbooks call [[inconsistent]]. Slide line 2 onto line 1, as `y − 2x = 1`, and `1 = 1` is true everywhere: endless solutions, called [[redundancy]].

pages.name: Last one
pages.why: This time line 1 says what x equals, so swap it in for x, giving `(2y − 1) + y = 8`. Then `3y − 1 = 8` and y = 3, so `x = 2 × 3 − 1 = 5`. It checks in both, as `2 × 3 − 1 = 5` and `5 + 3 = 8`.
